title: Hosea 6:1–11
context: Chapter 6 opens with words of the people: “Come! Let’s return to the LORD” (6:1–3). They confess that the LORD who tore them will heal them, hope for revival (“After two days he will revive us”) and raising (“On the third day he will raise us up”), and resolve to “press on to know the LORD.” Readers differ on whether these words are sincere repentance, a shallow formula, or a model of return that the prophet sets before Israel. The LORD’s reply (6:4–6) laments that their love is “like a morning cloud” and declares, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” Jesus cites this line in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7, and both traditions read it as shared ground about empty worship. Verses 7–10 return to indictment: “like Adam” (6:7) may refer to the first man, to humanity, or to the town of Adam by the Jordan (compare Joshua 3:16), and the crimes in Gilead and on the road to Shechem (6:8–9) cannot be tied to known events with confidence. Verse 11 speaks of a harvest appointed for Judah, which may mean judgment or blessing. Many Christian readers have connected the “third day” of 6:2 with Christ’s resurrection; the New Testament does not quote the verse directly, and readers in both traditions hold that connection with varying confidence. Shared ground: both traditions read the chapter as a call to steadfast love and true knowledge of the LORD.

verses.text: “Come! Let’s return to the LORD; for he has torn us to pieces, and he will heal us; he has injured us, and he will bind up our wounds.
verses.arminianNotes: “Come! Let’s return to the LORD; for he has torn us to pieces, and he will heal us.” Arminian readers hear the language of genuine repentance, a call to turn that answers the LORD’s waiting in 5:15, though the LORD’s reply in verse 4 suggests that the turning proved shallow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the people confess the LORD as both the one who tore and the one who heals (compare Deuteronomy 32:39), and they see true return as the fruit of his grace. Shared ground: both traditions note that readers differ on whether these words are sincere repentance, a shallow formula, or a model the prophet sets before the people, and both hear in them a true confession of who the LORD is.

verses.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
verses.arminianNotes: “After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up.” Many read the numbers as a poetic way of saying that revival will come soon. Arminian readers within the Christian tradition often hear the language of national revival echoed more fully in Christ’s rising on the third day, while holding that link with care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also commonly see a typological connection to the resurrection of Christ, in whom Israel’s hope is gathered (compare 1 Corinthians 15:4), while affirming the verse’s primary reference to the restoration of the people. Shared ground: both read the verse first as national hope; the New Testament does not quote it directly, and readers in both hold the resurrection link as possible rather than certain.

verses.text: Let’s acknowledge the LORD. Let’s press on to know the LORD. As surely as the sun rises, the LORD will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Let’s press on to know the LORD.” The pursuit of knowledge answers the lack described in 4:1 and 4:6. Arminian readers stress the active effort called for and the confidence that the LORD will come “like the spring rain” to those who seek him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the certainty of the LORD’s coming, “As surely as the sun rises,” as grounded in his faithfulness rather than in the people’s effort. Shared ground: both traditions read the call to know the LORD as central to Hosea, see the rain imagery as life-giving and possibly as a rebuke to cults that credited rain to other gods, and note that the LORD’s reply tests the resolve.

verses.text: “Ephraim, what shall I do to you? Judah, what shall I do to you? For your love is like a morning cloud, and like the dew that disappears early.
verses.arminianNotes: “Ephraim, what shall I do to you? Judah, what shall I do to you?” The LORD speaks with something like parental anguish. Arminian readers take the question as a real expression of divine grief over love that vanishes “like a morning cloud,” a relational response to the people’s fickleness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same anguish and read it as God’s revealed attitude toward covenant faithlessness, held together with his unchanging purpose. Shared ground: both traditions take the lament with full seriousness and agree that Israel’s love proved as passing as the dew; how such language fits with God’s constancy is treated in the existing discussion at 1 Samuel 15:29.

verses.text: Therefore I have cut them to pieces with the prophets; I killed them with the words of my mouth. Your judgments are like a flash of lightning.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore I have cut them to pieces with the prophets; I killed them with the words of my mouth.” Arminian readers see God’s word through the prophets as cutting precisely because it calls for a response: the word that warns also condemns those who refuse it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the power of the prophetic word, which accomplishes what God intends, both wounding and judging (compare Hebrews 4:12). Shared ground: both traditions read the prophets’ words as the LORD’s own words, see judgment “like a flash of lightning” as bringing hidden things to light, and acknowledge that the last line is variously understood.

verses.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
verses.arminianNotes: “For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” Arminian readers hear the LORD ranking steadfast love and true knowledge of him above ritual, not abolishing sacrifice but exposing worship emptied of loyalty. They note that Jesus applies the line to mercy toward sinners and the needy in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the comparison as a Hebrew way of ranking priorities: the LORD commanded sacrifice, but without covenant loyalty it is worthless (compare 1 Samuel 15:22). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a rebuke of empty worship, both see Jesus’ use of it in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7 as applying its priority of mercy, and neither finds a division between them here.

verses.text: But they, like Adam, have broken the covenant. They were unfaithful to me there.
verses.arminianNotes: “But they, like Adam, have broken the covenant. They were unfaithful to me there.” Arminian readers note that “Adam” may refer to the first man, to humanity generally, or to the town of Adam by the Jordan (compare Joshua 3:16), and that “there” suggests a place. On any reading, Israel’s breach is a free betrayal of a relationship the LORD established.
verses.reformedNotes: Many Reformed readers have historically seen a reference to the first man here, and some cite the verse in support of a covenant with Adam in Eden, while others in the tradition prefer the place reading. Shared ground: both traditions acknowledge that the verse can be read either way, and both affirm Adam’s fall and its consequences (see the existing discussion at Romans 5:12) apart from this verse.

verses.text: Gilead is a city of those who work iniquity; it is stained with blood.
verses.arminianNotes: “Gilead is a city of those who work iniquity; it is stained with blood.” Gilead usually names a region east of the Jordan; here it may stand for a town in that region or for its people. Arminian readers see the violence as the fruit of the broken covenant in verse 7, with responsibility borne by those who chose it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the bloodstain a public witness to guilt the LORD will not overlook; some connect the verse with the Gileadites who joined the coup in 2 Kings 15:25, though the link is uncertain. Shared ground: both traditions treat the identification and any historical event cautiously, and both read the verse as a charge of violence among God’s people.

verses.text: As gangs of robbers wait to ambush a man, so the company of priests murder on the path toward Shechem, committing shameful crimes.
verses.arminianNotes: “As gangs of robbers wait to ambush a man, so the company of priests murder on the path toward Shechem.” Arminian readers see the horror of those charged with holiness acting as bandits, a betrayal of office that they chose and own. Shechem was a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7), which may sharpen the charge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see corruption at the center of religious life: priests have become predators, and the LORD names their “shameful crimes.” Shared ground: both traditions note that the events behind the verse are unknown and that some take the language figuratively, and both read it as a grave indictment of priestly corruption in the northern kingdom.

verses.text: In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing. There is prostitution in Ephraim. Israel is defiled.
verses.arminianNotes: “In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing.” Arminian readers emphasize that the LORD sees what Israel has done and names it plainly; the prostitution language again describes covenant unfaithfulness, here as a settled condition in Ephraim rather than an occasional lapse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the divine verdict “Israel is defiled,” which repeats 5:3, as God’s authoritative judgment on the nation’s spiritual state. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, see the “horrible thing” as idolatry and its fruits, and note how the repeated language ties this indictment back to the charge that opened chapter 5.

verses.text: “Also, Judah, there is a harvest appointed for you, when I restore the fortunes of my people.
verses.arminianNotes: “Also, Judah, there is a harvest appointed for you.” Arminian readers note that the harvest may mean judgment, as elsewhere in the prophets (compare Joel 3:13), or future blessing; either way, Judah is not exempt from accountability, even as the LORD speaks of restoring his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the closing phrase, “when I restore the fortunes of my people,” as the LORD’s sovereign intention to restore beyond judgment. Shared ground: both traditions acknowledge that “harvest” can be read as judgment or blessing, note that some readers attach the closing phrase to 7:1, and see the LORD’s purpose to restore as the horizon of his judgments.
